system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 8 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2132-12-21 14:00:00 to 2132-12-28 18:48:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of morbid obesity, diabetes, chronic venous insufficiency, and heart failure was admitted after sustaining a traumatic wound to her right lower leg from a fall at her rehabilitation facility. The wound was deep, involving muscle and fascia, and she was admitted to vascular surgery for management. Her admission was complicated by acute kidney injury with elevated creatinine, likely due to dehydration, and a multidrug-resistant E. coli urinary tract infection sensitive only to meropenem. She was hydrated, her oral diabetes medications were held initially, and IV meropenem was started. After 24 hours of compression, she underwent debridement and VAC placement. Her kidney function improved, diabetes medications were resumed, and a PICC line was placed for outpatient antibiotic therapy. The wound developed healthy granulation tissue, and she was discharged to extended care with plans for readmission for skin grafting. She was stable, afebrile, and in good condition at discharge.
problems: Open wound of knee, leg [except thigh], and ankle, complicated
Urinary tract infection, site not specified
Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Other and unspecified Escherichia coli [E. coli]
Infection with microorganisms resistant to penicillins

Division of Vascular and Endovascular Surgery Discharge 
Instructions
 
What to expect when you go home:

1. It is normal to feel tired, this will last for ___ weeks 

·You should get up out of bed every day and gradually increase 
your activity each day 

·Increase your activities as you can tolerate- do not do too 
much right away!

2. It is normal to have swelling of the leg you were operated 
on:

·Avoid prolonged periods of standing or sitting without your 
legs elevated

3. It is normal to have a decreased appetite, your appetite will 
return with time 

·You will probably lose your taste for food and lose some weight 


·Eat small frequent meals

·It is important to eat nutritious food options (high fiber, 
lean meats, vegetables/fruits, low fat, low cholesterol) to 
maintain your strength and assist in wound healing

·To avoid constipation: eat a high fiber diet and use stool 
softener while taking pain medication

What activities you can and cannot do:

·No driving until post-op visit and you are no longer taking 
pain medications

·You may shower (unless you have stitches or foot incisions) no 
direct spray on incision, let the soapy water run over incision, 
rinse and pat dry. Cover the graft sites with tagederms when 
showering for the next week. Do not directly clean the graft 
site in the shower. 

·Take all the medications you were taking before surgery, unless 
otherwise directed

·Call and schedule an appointment to be seen in 2 weeks for 
staple/suture removal

What to report to office:

·Redness that extends away from your incision

·A sudden increase in pain that is not controlled with pain 
medication

·A sudden change in the ability to move or use your leg or the 
ability to feel your leg

·Temperature greater than 100.5F for 24 hours

·Bleeding, new or increased drainage from incision or white, 
yellow or green drainage from graft site and donor site.

 
Followup Instructions:
___

procedures.long_title: Other skin graft to other sites

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Patel, one of your surgical doctors. You’re here today for a skin graft on your right leg wound. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’m okay, just a little nervous. The wound’s been slow to heal, and I’m worried it won’t take.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely understandable. We’ve reviewed your history, and because of your diabetes and poor circulation, healing has been tough. But this graft is the next step to help it close properly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt? And what exactly are you doing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll put you to sleep, so you won’t feel anything. First, we’ll clean out any dead tissue—that’s called debridement. Then we’ll take a thin layer of skin from another area and place it over the wound.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, so you’re taking skin from somewhere else? Where?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Usually from your thigh. It’s a split-thickness graft, so it’s very thin and will heal well there. The main goal is to give your leg wound a better chance to heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. And after? What happens?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go back to your room, on bed rest for a few days. We’ll put a wound vacuum—VAC—on it to help the graft stay in place and prevent infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that from last time. It helps with healing, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It removes fluid and keeps the area clean. You’ll also get antibiotics to prevent infection, and we’ll monitor your heart and kidneys closely because of your other conditions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My heart’s been okay lately. But I know I have to be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we see you’re on several medications for heart failure, blood pressure, and diabetes. We’ll keep those managed carefully. For now, we’ll start IV fluids and keep you NPO—nothing by mouth—until after surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. When’s the surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Later this afternoon. The team is prepping the OR now. I’ll come back before we take you down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. You’re back from surgery. Everything went well—debridement and graft were successful. The VAC is in place at 75 mmHg. You’re doing great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Is the graft sticking?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s too early to say for sure, but it looks good so far. We’ll keep you on bed rest for a few days to protect it. We’ve also placed a Foley catheter to help with mobility issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I figured. It’s hard to get up with my size and breathing issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring your oxygen closely. You’re on 3 liters, and your lungs sound clear. We also checked a chest X-ray to confirm your PICC line is still in place—it is.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want any infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve stopped the antibiotics since it was just for prevention. Your labs look stable—creatinine is 1.3, which is normal for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Manageable. I took the acetaminophen they gave me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep that going. You can start sipping water and we’ll advance to a light diet if you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have some juice? I’m really thirsty.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Let’s start with small sips of water. If no nausea, we’ll try juice later. Your diabetes meds are on hold for now—we’re watching your glucose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, I had some chest tightness last night. Left side. It’s gone now, but I was scared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I saw the note. We did an EKG and checked troponin and CK-MB. Everything was normal, and your EKG looks the same as before surgery. It was likely musculoskeletal, but we’re keeping an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. My heart’s always a worry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know. That’s why we’re being cautious. Your urine output is good—over 50 cc per hour—so your kidneys are handling things well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine went up a little—to 1.6 today. But your urine output is still strong, so we don’t think it’s acute kidney injury. We’re not giving a fluid bolus because of your heart history, but we’re watching closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that bad? My last admission was for kidney issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a small rise, and given your history, we’re cautious. But no signs of overload or dehydration. It may just be a blip. We’ll recheck tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your creatinine is back down to 1.1. Looks like it was temporary. Your graft site is also looking stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Can I start moving a bit?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. Still bed rest. But we’ll reassess in a day or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today we’ll remove the VAC to check the graft. If it’s holding, we can start getting you up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous. What if it didn’t take?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll know soon. But your wound looked well-vascularized in the last exam, which is a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—the graft is intact and healthy. No signs of necrosis. We’re discontinuing the VAC and removing the Foley.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, thank goodness. I can finally get up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, activity as tolerated. Physical therapy will come by to help you walk safely. We’ll also restart your glargine insulin at 12 units tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve missed moving around.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well with PT yesterday. Your leg is stable, and you’re healing well. We’re planning to discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: To the rehab center again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, extended care. You’ll continue wound care there, and we’ll see you in two weeks to remove staples.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What meds will I be on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most of your usual ones—lisinopril, metoprolol, furosemide, simvastatin, pantoprazole, and glargine. Plus aspirin daily and heparin shots for blood clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And pain medicine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Acetaminophen and oxycodone for breakthrough pain. But don’t drive while taking it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Any restrictions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep the leg elevated, avoid standing too long. You can shower—just cover the graft with a Tegaderm and don’t scrub it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And when do I call the doctor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you have fever over 100.5, increased redness, sudden pain, or drainage from the graft. Also, weigh yourself daily—call if you gain more than 3 pounds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Final check before discharge. You’re afebrile, pain is controlled, and your graft looks excellent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready. Nervous, but ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done great. Keep up with your care, eat well, and follow up in two weeks. You’re on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I really appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—should I keep using the CPAP?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially with your obesity hypoventilation and sleep apnea. It helps your breathing and heart. We know you’ve had trouble before, but please try to use it nightly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do my best. I know it’s important.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s all we ask. Keep working on it. Your health depends on these small steps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Just keep following the plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I want to get better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And you are. This graft is a big step forward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad I came back for it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: So are we. It gives your wound the best chance to heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll take care of it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the spirit. We’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Looking forward to it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it easy, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright, the transport team will get you ready to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Get some rest and keep healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with multiple comorbidities, including morbid obesity, diabetes, congestive heart failure, atrial fibrillation, and obstructive sleep apnea, was admitted for a planned split-thickness skin graft to treat a non-healing right lower extremity wound sustained two weeks prior. She underwent successful debridement and grafting, with a wound vacuum placed postoperatively. Her recovery was complicated by a transient rise in creatinine to 1.6 on postoperative day 3, which resolved spontaneously without intervention, and a brief episode of left-sided chest pain that was ruled out for cardiac ischemia. The graft remained intact, and she was mobilized on postoperative day 6. She was discharged to extended care with instructions for wound care, activity progression, and follow-up in two weeks for staple removal. At discharge, she was afebrile, hemodynamically stable, and in good condition.
